Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
• 48-year-old male with 3-day history of acute watery diarrhoea (5–6 episodes/day) preceded by brief vomiting; clinical picture most consistent with viral gastroenteritis.

History:
• Presenting complaint & timeline: Sudden onset of vomiting (2 episodes) followed within hours by watery diarrhoea; diarrhoea ongoing ×3 days.  
• Symptoms: Watery, loose stools, no visible blood/mucus, no abdominal pain, subjective low-grade fever only on day 1, marked weakness and thirst/dehydration, poor appetite. No headache or myalgia.  
• Pertinent negatives: No recent antibiotics, hospital stay, travel, high-risk food, or sick contacts.  
• PMH: Intermittent asthma.  
• Medications: Salbutamol (blue) inhaler PRN; no other regular drugs.  
• Allergies: Denies known drug allergies.  
• Family history: Father – hypertension, deceased due to colorectal cancer; Mother – type 2 diabetes.  
• Social / preventive: Lives alone, software engineer; non-smoker; alcohol socially and infrequently. No mention of recent vaccinations.

Examination:
• Telephone consult – no vitals or physical examination performed/reported.

Impression:
• Viral gastroenteritis (most likely norovirus) – abrupt onset, self-limited course, watery diarrhoea without blood or severe pain, initial vomiting.  
• Alternative considerations (less likely):  
  – Bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis (Salmonella/Campylobacter/ETEC): lack of abdominal cramps or recalled food exposure.  
  – Clostridioides difficile infection: unlikely without recent antibiotics/hospitalisation.

Plan:
• Supportive care: Encourage generous oral fluids; purchase oral rehydration salts (e.g., Dioralyte) for electrolyte replacement.  
• Symptom control: Paracetamol as needed for fever or malaise.  
• Activity: Remain off work until diarrhoea-free for 24–48 h; likely need 1–2 additional days’ rest.  
• Warning signs / follow-up: Return for review if no improvement or worsening after 5–7 days, inability to keep fluids down, signs of severe dehydration, bloody stools, high fever, or abdominal pain.  
• No routine labs or imaging indicated at this stage.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: Objective vitals (temperature, BP, HR), physical examination (abdominal exam, hydration status), immunisation status (e.g., COVID/flu), detailed medication list (dose/frequency of inhaler).  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear but limited; telephone format precluded exam and vitals; otherwise coherent history.
